body:
Religion and philosophy in Indian culture

Indian religious and philosophical traditions developed through centuries of inquiry into human existence, the nature of reality, moral conduct and the purpose of life. They influenced literature, education, sculpture, architecture, music, festivals, social institutions and reform movements.

Indian philosophy is not a single system of thought. Different traditions accept different sources of knowledge and offer different explanations of the soul, the universe, suffering and liberation. Some emphasise ritual, others knowledge, meditation, ethical conduct or devotion.

The Vedic tradition

The Vedas constitute the oldest surviving corpus of Indian religious literature. They were composed in Vedic Sanskrit and preserved through carefully organised oral transmission.

The early Vedic period is generally placed around 1500–1000 BCE, and the later Vedic period around 1000–500 BCE. These are approximate historical periods rather than exact boundaries.

VedaPrincipal contents
RigvedaHymns addressed to various deities; the oldest Veda
SamavedaVerses arranged for melodic chanting during rituals
YajurvedaSacrificial formulas and instructions for rituals
AtharvavedaHymns, charms, prayers, healing and aspects of everyday life

Early Vedic worship included deities associated with natural and cosmic phenomena. Indra was associated with storms and warfare, Agni with fire and sacrifice, Varuna with cosmic and moral order, and Soma with a sacred ritual drink and its associated deity.

The performance of yajna, or sacrifice, was an important religious practice. Offerings were made into sacred fire while hymns and formulas were recited. Sacrifices could be performed for prosperity, health, offspring and political authority. Later Vedic rulers performed elaborate ceremonies such as the Rajasuya and Ashvamedha.

Rita and cosmic order

Rita refers to the underlying cosmic and moral order that maintains harmony in the universe. It is associated particularly with Varuna in Vedic thought. The concept contributed to later Indian ideas concerning truth, duty and righteous conduct.

The four major categories of Vedic literature

  • Samhitas: Collections of hymns, prayers and ritual formulas.
  • Brahmanas: Prose explanations of sacrifices and their religious significance.
  • Aranyakas: Texts concerned with the symbolic and contemplative aspects of ritual, traditionally associated with forest study.
  • Upanishads: Philosophical inquiries into ultimate reality, the self, knowledge and liberation.

The Upanishadic tradition

The Upanishads form the concluding philosophical portion of Vedic literature. They investigate questions such as whether something permanent exists beyond bodily existence, what causes rebirth and how human beings can attain liberation.

Many Upanishadic teachings examine the relationship between Atman, the inner or individual self, and Brahman, the ultimate reality underlying existence. Several influential Upanishadic passages express their fundamental unity, although later philosophical schools interpret this relationship differently.

The Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya Upanishads are among the important early Upanishads. Philosophical knowledge was frequently presented through dialogues between teachers and students.

Yajnavalkya was a prominent Upanishadic thinker. Gargi participated in philosophical debates, while Maitreyi is associated with inquiries into the self and immortality. Their presence demonstrates that women also contributed to ancient Indian intellectual traditions, despite wider restrictions on access to formal learning.

Fundamental concepts

ConceptMeaning
DharmaRighteous conduct, duty and the principles sustaining moral or social order
KarmaAction and its consequences
SamsaraThe continuing cycle of birth, death and rebirth
MokshaLiberation from the cycle of rebirth
AtmanThe self, as understood in different philosophical traditions
BrahmanUltimate reality in Upanishadic and Vedantic thought

These concepts became influential across Indian intellectual traditions, but their meanings are not identical in every school. Buddhism, for example, accepts karma and rebirth while rejecting the doctrine of an eternal, unchanging individual self.

Brahman, Brahma and Brahmana

Brahman is ultimate reality in Vedantic philosophy. Brahma is the deity associated with creation. A Brahmana may refer to a member of the Brahmana varna or to a category of Vedic ritual literature, depending on the context.

Purusharthas and stages of life

Classical Hindu thought identifies 4 broad aims of human life, known as Purusharthas: dharma, artha or material prosperity, kama or legitimate enjoyment and desire, and moksha or spiritual liberation.

The traditional Ashrama system describes 4 stages of life: Brahmacharya (studentship), Grihastha (household life), Vanaprastha (gradual withdrawal from household responsibilities) and Sannyasa (renunciation). Historically, the prescribed application of this system varied according to social status and gender.

Prelims focus

  • Rigveda is the oldest of the 4 Vedas.
  • Brahmanas primarily explain sacrificial rituals.
  • Upanishads emphasise philosophical knowledge and ultimate reality.
  • Gargi, Maitreyi and Yajnavalkya belong to the Upanishadic intellectual tradition.
  • The 4 Purusharthas are dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
  • Trap: Brahman and Brahma do not refer to the same concept.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 84–85 and 110; NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, pp. 67–74; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 10, Social Science, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, pp. 30–31, English-medium online textbook extract, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Vedic and Upanishadic Foundations of Indian Thought

body:
Meaning of Darshana

The Sanskrit term Darshana refers to a philosophical viewpoint or system through which reality and human existence are understood. Indian thinkers developed several Darshanas to investigate knowledge, consciousness, matter, moral action and liberation.

Astika and Nastika traditions

Classical Indian philosophical systems are conventionally classified according to whether they accept the authority of the Vedas.

  • Astika: Systems accepting Vedic authority. The 6 classical Astika schools are Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Purva Mimamsa and Vedanta.
  • Nastika: Systems not accepting Vedic authority. Buddhism, Jainism and Charvaka are prominent examples. The historical Ajivika tradition also developed outside Vedic orthodoxy.

In this classification, Astika does not necessarily mean belief in a creator God, and Nastika does not necessarily mean rejection of every spiritual belief. The decisive distinction is acceptance or rejection of Vedic authority.

The Shad Darshanas

The 6 classical Astika systems are collectively known as the Shad Darshanas. Each developed over generations, although particular sages are traditionally associated with its foundation or principal text.

SchoolTraditional proponentPrincipal textMain emphasis
NyayaGautamaNyaya SutraLogic and valid knowledge
VaisheshikaKanadaVaisheshika SutraCategories of reality and atomism
SamkhyaKapilaSamkhya Karika by IshvarakrishnaPurusha and Prakriti
YogaPatanjaliYoga SutraDiscipline of mind and body
Purva MimamsaJaiminiMimamsa SutraVedic duties and rituals
VedantaBadarayanaBrahma SutraUltimate reality and liberation

Nyaya and Vaisheshika

Nyaya: reasoning and knowledge

Nyaya investigates how reliable knowledge is obtained and how false conclusions can be avoided. Its major contribution is the systematic development of logic, inference and argument.

Classical Nyaya recognises 4 principal means of valid knowledge, called Pramanas: perception (Pratyaksha), inference (Anumana), comparison (Upamana) and reliable verbal testimony (Shabda).

Observing smoke and concluding that a fire exists on the basis of an established relationship between smoke and fire illustrates inference. Directly observing the fire illustrates perception.

Vaisheshika: the nature of reality

Vaisheshika, associated with Kanada, investigates the categories of existence, including substances, qualities and actions. It is particularly known for its theory that material objects are composed of extremely small, indivisible units called atoms.

This is an ancient philosophical theory of matter and should not be confused with the experimentally established atomic theory of modern science.

Samkhya and Yoga

Samkhya: consciousness and nature

Samkhya distinguishes between 2 fundamental principles:

  • Purusha: Pure consciousness, distinct from material nature.
  • Prakriti: Primordial nature, from which the material world and mental faculties evolve.

According to Samkhya, Prakriti operates through 3 qualities or Gunas: Sattva, associated with clarity and harmony; Rajas, associated with activity and restlessness; and Tamas, associated with inertia and obscurity. Liberation involves recognising the fundamental distinction between Purusha and Prakriti.

Kapila is traditionally regarded as its founder. The surviving classical Samkhya Karika was composed by Ishvarakrishna.

Yoga: practical spiritual discipline

Patanjali systematised classical Yoga in the Yoga Sutra. Yoga shares much of the philosophical framework of Samkhya but gives particular attention to controlling mental activity and attaining liberation through disciplined practice.

The 8 limbs of Patanjali's Yoga are collectively called Ashtanga Yoga:

  1. Yama: ethical restraints.
  2. Niyama: personal observances.
  3. Asana: bodily posture.
  4. Pranayama: regulation of breathing.
  5. Pratyahara: withdrawal of the senses.
  6. Dharana: concentration.
  7. Dhyana: meditation.
  8. Samadhi: deep meditative absorption.

Classical Yoga is therefore a comprehensive ethical and philosophical discipline, not merely a system of physical exercise.

Purva Mimamsa and Vedanta

Purva Mimamsa, associated with Jaimini, investigates the interpretation of Vedic injunctions and the performance of prescribed duties and rituals. It places considerable importance on the ritual portions of Vedic literature.

Vedanta, also called Uttara Mimamsa, concentrates on philosophical knowledge, particularly the teachings of the Upanishads. Badarayana's Brahma Sutra is its foundational systematic text. Different Vedanta schools developed distinct interpretations of Brahman and the individual soul.

The traditional complementary pairs

  • Nyaya and Vaisheshika: reasoning, knowledge and the nature of existence.
  • Samkhya and Yoga: philosophical analysis and spiritual discipline.
  • Purva Mimamsa and Vedanta: Vedic ritual interpretation and philosophical inquiry.

Prelims focus

  • Gautama is associated with Nyaya and Kanada with Vaisheshika.
  • Kapila is associated with Samkhya and Patanjali with Yoga.
  • Samkhya distinguishes Purusha from Prakriti.
  • Jaimini is associated with Purva Mimamsa.
  • Badarayana is associated with the Brahma Sutra and Vedanta.
  • Trap: The Astika classification is based on Vedic authority, not compulsory belief in a creator God.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, p. 67; NCERT, Class 11, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Chapter 2, Indian Philosophical Systems, SATHEE IIT Kanpur online edition; National Curriculum Framework for School Education, 2023, Box 1.3i, Indian Schools of Thought; University of Calicut, The Systems of Indian Philosophy, introduction; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: The Six Classical Schools of Indian Philosophy

body:
The rise of Shramana traditions

Around the middle of the 1st millennium BCE, northern India experienced important changes, including urban growth, expanding trade and the emergence of powerful kingdoms. The Gangetic plains became centres of religious debate and philosophical inquiry.

Several teachers questioned the authority of Vedic rituals, hereditary social privileges and the idea that sacrifices alone could ensure spiritual progress. Wandering ascetics and seekers associated with such traditions were known as Shramanas.

Buddhism, Jainism and Ajivika developed within this broader intellectual environment. They shared certain concerns about existence and liberation but differed significantly in their explanations and methods.

Gautama Buddha

Siddhartha Gautama, who belonged to the Shakya clan, became known as the Buddha after attaining enlightenment. He lived during the period of religious and intellectual change conventionally associated with the 6th century BCE. His exact birth and death years remain subjects of historical debate.

According to Buddhist tradition, awareness of old age, sickness and death encouraged Siddhartha to renounce worldly life. After experimenting with severe asceticism, he rejected both extreme bodily hardship and excessive enjoyment.

PlaceEventPresent location
LumbiniBirthNepal
Bodh GayaEnlightenmentBihar
SarnathFirst sermonUttar Pradesh
KushinagarMahaparinirvanaUttar Pradesh

The first sermon at Sarnath is associated with the Dharmachakra Pravartana, or setting in motion of the wheel of Dharma.

The Four Noble Truths

Buddhist teaching begins with the problem of Dukkha, which includes suffering, dissatisfaction and the instability of conditioned existence.

  1. Dukkha: Conditioned existence is characterised by suffering and dissatisfaction.
  2. Samudaya: Craving, attachment and ignorance sustain suffering.
  3. Nirodha: Suffering can cease through the elimination of its causes.
  4. Magga: The Noble Eightfold Path provides the way towards the cessation of suffering.

The Noble Eightfold Path

The path combines wisdom, moral conduct and mental discipline.

CategoryComponents
WisdomRight view and right intention
Moral conductRight speech, right action and right livelihood
Mental disciplineRight effort, right mindfulness and right concentration

The Middle Way avoids the extremes of sensual indulgence and severe self-mortification. It is a disciplined path, not an instruction to avoid all effort or moral restraint.

Essential Buddhist philosophical concepts

  • Anicca: Impermanence. Conditioned things arise, change and cease.
  • Anatta: The absence of a permanent, unchanging individual self.
  • Dukkha: Suffering or dissatisfaction associated with conditioned existence.
  • Dependent origination: Phenomena arise through causes and conditions rather than existing independently.
  • Nirvana: The extinguishing of craving, hatred and ignorance, bringing liberation from the cycle of suffering and rebirth.

Buddhism accepts the moral consequences of intentional actions through its doctrine of karma. However, continuity across rebirth does not require an eternal soul in Buddhist philosophy.

A major philosophical distinction

Jainism accepts enduring individual souls. Buddhism rejects an eternal, unchanging self. Both recognise karma and rebirth, but they explain these concepts differently.

Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha

The 3 Buddhist refuges, also called the Triple Gem or Triratna, are the Buddha, the Dhamma or teaching, and the Sangha or community.

The Buddhist Sangha developed as an organised monastic community. Monks were known as Bhikkhus and nuns as Bhikkhunis. According to Buddhist tradition, Mahapajapati Gotami became the first Buddhist nun after Ananda appealed for the admission of women into the order.

Monks and nuns depended upon lay supporters for necessities, while providing religious instruction and preserving teachings. Merchants, rulers and ordinary householders supported monasteries through donations.

Language and accessibility

Buddhist teachers communicated in languages understood by ordinary people. Early Buddhist literature was preserved in several Middle Indo-Aryan linguistic traditions, particularly Pali in the Theravada tradition. Sanskrit became important in later Buddhist literature.

Prelims focus

  • Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar correspond to birth, enlightenment, first sermon and death respectively.
  • The Four Noble Truths culminate in the Noble Eightfold Path.
  • Anicca means impermanence; Anatta means absence of a permanent self.
  • Buddhist Triratna consists of Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.
  • Mahapajapati Gotami is traditionally recognised as the first Buddhist nun.
  • Trap: Buddhism does not teach severe self-mortification as the necessary path to liberation.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts I, 2018–19, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, pp. 65–72; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History Part I, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 84–94; NIOS, Senior Secondary History, Lesson 5, From Janapadas to Empire, section on Buddhist teachings, consulted 26 November 2026.]
